Q: Autofilling data based on shared URL in Google Forms / Google Spreadsheets A:

You can create prefilled URLs that open the form so that some of the fields have a value filled in automatically. You'll need to create a URLs for each location ID. When the user opens the URL in a web browser through the QR code that uses that URL, the form opens, and the location ID is already filled in.

The location ID question will by default be visible to the user, and they can edit it at will. To hide the location ID field, place it in a section, and jump over the section using the "go to section based on answer" feature.

See Send a form with pre-filled answers.

Q: How do I randomize what rows I import from an SAS file? A:

I'll use sample data from the haven package itself, since it doesn't matter if the real file is 100GB or 131KB (as here).

I'm assuming that you cannot read in the entire file at once. (If you could, then there are numerous easy ways to sample rows from an in-memory dataset.) Also, since I don't have a 100GB file (and do not regularly work with them), I do not know that with skip= and n_max= if the function still reads other than the desired rows into memory; if it does then there may not be an easy way to do what you need.

I believe haven::read_sas does not provide any built-in way to randomly sample rows. As such, I think the best thing we can do is randomize where we start loading data (what row number) and then accept that the 1000 rows will be consecutive.

(I'll demonstrate on a single file, I assume you will be able to adapt to your lapply(files, ...).)

The sample data is just a SAS file of iris data, it has 150 rows and five columns. I'll load 3 rows from random start-rows:

path <- system.file("examples", "iris.sas7bdat", package = "haven")
haven::read_sas(path, skip = sample(150, 1), n_max = 3)
# # A tibble: 3 × 5
#   Sepal_Length Sepal_Width Petal_Length Petal_Width Species
#          <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>  
# 1          5.6         2.9          3.6         1.3 versic 
# 2          6.7         3.1          4.4         1.4 versic 
# 3          5.6         3            4.5         1.5 versic 
haven::read_sas(path, skip = sample(150, 1), n_max = 3)
# # A tibble: 3 × 5
#   Sepal_Length Sepal_Width Petal_Length Petal_Width Species
#          <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>  
# 1          5.5         2.4          3.8         1.1 versic 
# 2          5.5         2.4          3.7         1   versic 
# 3          5.8         2.7          3.9         1.2 versic 
haven::read_sas(path, skip = sample(150, 1), n_max = 3)
# # A tibble: 3 × 5
#   Sepal_Length Sepal_Width Petal_Length Petal_Width Species
#          <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>  
# 1          5.8         2.7          3.9         1.2 versic 
# 2          6           2.7          5.1         1.6 versic 
# 3          5.4         3            4.5         1.5 versic

If you do not know the total number of rows, I think you have two options:

  1. Wrap read_sas() and if it does not return the 1000 rows, then immediately re-sample. If the read operation is slow (due to the size of the file) then you might occasionally "feel" this. Perhaps this:

    read_sas_minrows <- function(path, ..., min_rows = 1, iters = 3) {
  iter <- iters
  while (iter > 0) {
    dat <- haven::read_sas(path, ...)
    if (nrow(dat) >= min_rows) break
    message(sprintf("attempt %d/%d returned %d rows, reattempting",
                    iters-iter+1, iters, nrow(dat)))
    iter <- iter - 1L
  }
  if (iter == 0) stop(sprintf("read_sas_minrows: no call returned at least %d rows", iters))
  dat
}

### unlikely to fail
read_sas_minrows(path, skip = sample(150, 1), n_max = 3, min_rows = 3)
# # A tibble: 3 × 5
#   Sepal_Length Sepal_Width Petal_Length Petal_Width Species
#          <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl> <chr>  
# 1          6.2         2.9          4.3         1.3 versic 
# 2          5.1         2.5          3           1.1 versic 
# 3          5.7         2.8          4.1         1.3 versic 

### impossible condition n_max < min_rows, just to show it work
read_sas_minrows(path, skip=sample(150,1), n_max=3, min_rows=4)
# attempt 1/3 returned 3 rows, reattempting
# attempt 2/3 returned 3 rows, reattempting
# attempt 3/3 returned 3 rows, reattempting
# Error in read_sas_minrows(path, skip = sample(150, 1), n_max = 3, min_rows = 4): 
#   read_sas_minrows: no call returned at least 3 rows

  2. Use a simple binary-search to empirically find the number of rows. For instance, something like this might give you a good number (assuming that the act of reading 1 row is not "expensive"):

    known_rows <- 1L   # initial condition, if you have a known min then use that
try_rows <- 1e5    # your best guess
stop_margin <- 10 # if this is > 1, we do not need an "exact number of rows", just ball-park
while (TRUE) {
  message("attempting ", try_rows)
  dat <- haven::read_sas(path, skip=try_rows, n_max=1)
  if (nrow(dat) > 0) {
    a <- try_rows
    try_rows <- try_rows + ceiling((try_rows - known_rows) / 2)
    known_rows <- a
    next
  }
  if ((try_rows - known_rows) <= stop_margin) break
  try_rows <- ceiling(known_rows + (try_rows - known_rows) / 2); try_rows
}
# attempting 1e+05
# attempting 50001
# attempting 25001
# attempting 12501
# attempting 6251
# attempting 3126
# attempting 1564
# attempting 783
# attempting 392
# attempting 197
# attempting 99
# attempting 148
# attempting 173
# attempting 161
# attempting 155
# this is within `stop_margin` of the true number of rows
try_rows
# [1] 155

Q: How to checkout a tag with GitPython A:

You can now clone with the tag checked out if you provide it as branch like so:

from git import Repo


TAG="v1.100.1"

Repo.clone_from(
    "{self.ssh_url}/{project}", project, 
    branch=TAG,
)

Python 3.12
gitpython==3.1.46

Q: How to use Google Material Symbols in Expo React Native A:

I created a script to extract the unicode code point map from Google Fonts: https://github.com/terros-inc/expo-material-symbols

This can then be used after adding the font that can be downloaded from Google's repo: https://github.com/google/material-design-icons/tree/master/variablefont

For example:

import glyphMap from './map.json'
const MaterialSymbols = createIconSet(glyphMap, 'Material Symbols Outlined', 'MaterialSymbolsOutlined.ttf')

Q: Referencing after filter results A:

One possible way to solve this is to add a help column with the SUBTOTAL function to indicate visible rows. This function (in the Visible column) can refer to any column of the table that does not contain blank cells, for example:
=SUBTOTAL(3,[@Total])
The sum of visible entries in the Total column is obtained from the formula:
=SUMIFS(Table2[Total],Table2[Dept_ID],G14,Table2[Visible],1)

Q: Time function for Plasma simulation A:

tl;dr: I propose a sawtooth wave, rather than the triangle wave you depicted.

Consider a Hollywood film of a car speeding down the highway. At some speeds the spokes of the wheel will syncronize with the camera's frame rate, and they will appear stationary. Or even start to apparently move backwards.

More relevant to your project, consider a desktop "drip machine". It lets out water drips at regular intervals, falling perhaps a foot into a pan. We illuminate the drips with a stroboscope, and adjust the rate of flashing to match the rate of dripping. Then, as with the previous example, we can adjust a little bit up or down to make the water droplets appear to hover, fall very slowly, or even "fall" upwards. Of course, the droplets are never stationary, but the next droplet moves into the same Y-coordinate position just as the next flash happens, and visual fusion completes the illusion.

You proposed some T_end parameter that you found convenient, hoping it would be long enough to start to see stability.

I claim that you want to introduce impurity particles at regular intervals, just as with the water droplets, and use a sawtooth waveform which matches that interval. Or perhaps a multiple of the interval, so you'll see multiple particles at once.

You're hoping to see how instability around the repeated particle pathway impacts stability of the surrounding plasma.
